title: Report on Studying at Tulane University School of Medicine
paragraphs: I recently studied abroad for about two months at Tulane University in New Orleans, Louisiana, in the US. New Orleans is the birthplace of jazz and is also known as one of the best gourmet cities in America with its own distinctive food culture, and it was a lovely city with the cheerful, lively atmosphere of the South. This study abroad was two months that were hard but fun, and the most stimulating of my life.

For the first two weeks I rotated with the pulmonology consult team. Pulmonology is divided into the MICU and the consult team, and the consult team responds for a certain period when there are pulmonology requests from other departments. In the morning, I went on rounds with the fellow, took histories and examined patients together, and then went on rounds again with the attending. In my free time, I observed bronchoscopies and went to see outpatient clinics. The fellow also gave me homework every day, so I had many opportunities to read papers and present summaries, or to look up diseases and give presentations. Because I basically moved together with the fellow in charge, I could be taught various things one-on-one, and I think it was a good clerkship for the start of my study abroad. The fellow in charge was Asian, a doctor who graduated from a medical school in Asia, passed the USMLE and was training in the US. Because we were both Asian, the fellow felt a closeness to me, and we talked about various things. I heard a story that, like me, this doctor had had the opportunity to do a clerkship abroad as a medical student but could not go because their scores were not high enough, that they were frustrated by it, and so studied English hard and decided to obtain a US medical license. I was impressed by that effort and attitude toward learning, and my own motivation rose. In pulmonology there were doctors from various places of origin, including Thai, Indian, Chinese and Dominican doctors, and it was a very international team. Listening to doctors with various backgrounds was very helpful in thinking about what options I have for my future and what kind of career plans there are.

For the next two weeks I rotated through anesthesiology. Here too, the fellows and residents taught me various things one-on-one. I had chosen anesthesiology because I wanted to practise tracheal intubation, but at first I was told "you're an international student, so you can only observe," and I was not allowed to intubate. However, when I told the attending, "I did not come to observe. I came to do a clerkship. I have filled in the documents properly and obtained permission, so it is strange that I am not allowed to do it," I came to be allowed to intubate. I felt with my own body that it is important not to give up and to keep negotiating even after being told no once. Also, many Americans are difficult to intubate, so there were many chances to use LMAs, bronchoscopes and video laryngoscopes, and I was able to try intubation methods I had never seen in the Japanese polyclinic clerkships, which was very educational.

For the last two weeks I rotated through the stroke service of neurology. Because it is the department I hope to enter, I approached it with spirit, but my heart was immediately crushed. The stroke service is in charge of acute-phase treatment of cerebral infarction, so the clerkship is basically in the Neuro ICU. In the ICU, the attending, fellow, residents, fourth-year students and third-year students act as one team. Until then I had been taught one-on-one by a single doctor, and this was my first time doing a clerkship together with local medical students, and when I compared myself with them, my own shortcomings were exposed even more and I fell into self-loathing. Also, some doctors were not very friendly toward international students, and at first only I was not given patients, my name was not even on the list of students rotating, and I was the only one who did not receive the emails about the clerkship schedule. I was nearly crushed by the sense of isolation of being an international student and by the inferiority complex about my low English ability and lack of medical knowledge. I remember crying every day out of frustration. But I told myself again, "There is no point in comparing myself with the local students. Let me try to feel even a little growth within myself," and, not fearing failure and casting aside my embarrassment, I actively talked to the doctors and students and tried to absorb as much as I could. From the third day I was allowed to have patients, and I got the chance to present in front of the whole team on rounds every day. In the second week, a doctor said to me, "I'm thinking of discharging the patient today; I'd like to hear your opinion," and a student asked me, "The etiology of Mr. or Ms. so-and-so's cerebral infarction seems difficult. Do you know it?", and so I came to be treated as a member of the team. The clerkship in the Neuro ICU was truly hard and full of tears every day, but it was also the two weeks in which I grew the most.

I gained many things from this study abroad, but if I had to name one, it would be confidence. Besides the clerkships described above, many things did not go smoothly, such as the dormitory procedures, deciding on the clerkship departments, connecting to wifi and accessing the charts, and it was a series of hardships. But by not giving up and negotiating, I managed to overcome every difficulty. I think that experience led to the confidence that if you do your best, things will somehow work out. Also, seeing the local students' attitude in clerkships seemed to teach me the importance of having confidence in myself. The local students spoke up actively, not fearing mistakes, not only in lectures but also in conferences. I also saw scenes in which they raised objections about what they thought might be wrong, regardless of whether the other party was a doctor. Seeing such students, I reflected on how passive my own attitude in the polyclinic clerkships until then had been. And I felt that, in order to gain confidence in myself, I have to apply myself to my studies harder than ever.

I feel I experienced many things on this study abroad that I could never have experienced if I had stayed in Japan. Not only the improvement of my English ability, but also what I cultivated in these two months will surely nourish my life. I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to the International Collaboration Office and the Student Affairs staff who helped me with this study abroad, to my family and friends who cheered me on, to the people I met at my destination, and to everyone. Thank you very much.
